intro.uz: Dilnoza qishloqda fermer togʻasi Akmal bilan suvni qanday tejash haqida suhbatlashadi. Oʻqishdan oldin oʻylab koʻring: uyingizda suv qayerda behuda sarflanadi?

paragraphs.en: Dilnoza: Uncle Akmal, why are there black pipes lying along every row of your tomatoes? I don't remember them from last summer. Akmal: That's my new drip irrigation system. In the past, we used to flood the whole field with water from the canal. Now these thin pipes carry water straight to the roots of each plant, drop by drop.

Dilnoza: Does it really make such a big difference? Akmal: It does. When you flood a field in July, a lot of the water evaporates in the sun or runs off to places where nothing grows. With drip irrigation, much less is wasted. I have used less water this year, and my tomatoes have grown better than ever, because the soil doesn't get too wet or too dry.

Dilnoza: So why doesn't everyone in the village use it? Akmal: Setting it up costs money, and you have to keep the pipes clean, or they get blocked. Some farmers here are still waiting to see if it works. My neighbour said he would try it next year if my harvest was good.

Dilnoza: We don't have a field in Tashkent, but my teacher says families waste a lot of water too. Akmal: Your teacher is right. A dripping tap or a leaking toilet can waste a surprising amount of water, and it is usually easy to fix. Your aunt noticed that our kitchen tap had been dripping for weeks, so we finally changed the washer. It took ten minutes.

Dilnoza: What else can we do at home? Akmal: Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. Wash fruit in a bowl instead of under running water, and give that water to the plants afterwards. Water the garden early in the morning or in the evening, when it is cooler. In a dry region like ours, every bucket matters.
Dilnoza: I'm going to write a list and put it on our fridge as soon as I get home. Akmal: Good idea. And check under the kitchen sink while you're at it. Small leaks are very easy to miss.
